articles.title: Oscar-Winning Lawyering
articles.content:
许多人因在电影中饰演律师而获得奥斯卡奖，包括汤姆·汉克斯和蒂尔达·斯文顿。但在好莱坞早期，律师角色的表现却很难得到认可。谁是第一位因饰演律师而获得奥斯卡奖的演员？

**提示**：这一胜利开创了一个小传统，第二年最佳男主角奖也颁给了一个律师角色。

（原文来自：Above the Law）
articles.summary:
Many actors have won Academy Awards for portraying lawyers over the years including Tom Hanks and Tilda Swinton. But in the early days of Hollywood, attorney roles struggled to gain recognition. Who was the first actor to win an Oscar for portraying a lawyer?

Hint: It kicked off a little run, with the Best Actor Oscar going to a lawyer role the next year as well.

The post Oscar-Winning Lawyering appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Troutman Pepper Locke Will Pay Associates Market Compensation, Well, Some Of Them
articles.content:
It’s a match! With an asterisk… or two.
Troutman Pepper Locke is the latest firm to get on board with the salary scale Milbank set back in June, telling associates it will pay market — effective January 1, 2027. The firm is matching lockstep for associates in their first through fourth years, which puts those classes on a scale that starts at $235,000, as per the below.
Midlevel and senior associates are, as is the firm’s tradition, off the compensation grid entirely. That tradition goes back to the Locke Lord merger, when Troutman announced a comp model that paid market for first- and second-years and then sorted everyone senior to that onto a two-tier “standard” or “increased” scale. As per the firm’s announcement, only older associates on that higher tier will make the Milbank scale.
So credit where it’s due: the grid grew. It used to run out after year two, and now it runs through year four. Two additional class years of knowing what your paycheck will say is not nothing.
Then there’s the date. Milbank’s raises landed this summer. Troutman’s land January 1, which leaves associates doing the back half of 2026 at last year’s numbers. Troutman is not the first firm this cycle to match now and pay later, and it won’t be the last, but the firms picking that option aren’t really paying their associates top dollar.
Remember everyone, we depend on your tips to stay on top of important salary updates, so when your firm matches, please text us (646-820-8477) or email us (subject line: “[Firm Name] Matches”). Please include the memo if available. You can take a photo of the memo and send it via text or email if you don’t want to forward the original PDF or Word file.
And if you’d like to sign up for ATL’s Bonus Alerts (which is the alert list we also use for salary announcements), please scroll down and enter your email address in the box below this post. If you previously signed up for the bonus alerts, you don’t need to do anything. You’ll receive an email notification within minutes of each salary announcement that we publish. Thanks for all of your help!

articles.title: Utah Is Using Insurance Records To Catch Montana Loophole Tax Evaders Which Other States Could Follow
articles.content:
In previous columns, I have covered the “Montana Loophole,” where car owners would deliberately register their car outside of the state they reside in. People did this to avoid their home state’s sales taxes, annual registration fees, regular smog checks in some states, and in California’s case, to avoid mandatory and expensive emissions modification
While this strategy was initially used by owners of expensive sports cars and trailers, a recent Utah Tax Commission study showed that these days some of their residents are using this tactic for regular cars. Although only a tiny fraction of the population use this tactic, people publicly boasting on social media and online forums about never getting caught risks encouraging others to try.
As state legislatures become aware of the Montana Loophole, they have passed or proposed legislation to close it. For example, in California, Senate Bill 1406 (SB 1406) has passed the state legislature and Gov. Gavin Newsom is expected to sign it into law. SB 1406 would close the Montana Loophole by expanding California’s definition of who is a resident under state use tax law to include a shell company when at least one member of the business is a California resident. SB 1406 would also authorize tax agencies to impose tax liability on the individual members of a shell company.
The problem with SB 1406 and similar laws proposed in other states is that it requires the government to know that the improperly registered car exists, which is mostly done through law enforcement stopping suspicious vehicles. But police are reluctant to pull over people for simply having out-of-state plates because in most cases they have legal reasons for not doing so.
But Utah recently passed a law that has taken the police out of the equation and instead looks at a driver’s insurance records. Under this new law, if the Utah Tax Commission finds that a driver’s car is insured in Utah but is registered in another state, they will contact the owner and demand that the car be registered in Utah and pay registration fees and taxes. Alternatively, they can reply explaining why they are exempt. If they fail to do either, they will be subject to fines.
In about five months of work, the tax commission has brought in $1.6 million in sales tax and $32,540 in fines and that number is expected to double in another six months. Jason Gardner, deputy executive director of the Utah State Tax Commission believes even if this is not a huge moneymaker, it is worth it to make the system more fair.
If Utah’s law is successful in closing the loophole, expect other states to follow their lead. In California, it is estimated that cars fraudulently registered out of state is costing the state approximately $20 million per year in lost tax revenue.
States may also implement other strategies that rely less on police. States may establish a multistate reciprocity agreement where a car registered in one state but garaged in another could impose an additional fee equivalent to the registration fee in the home state. But some states (like Montana) probably won’t participate since the loophole benefits them financially. States could also implement automated license plate readers to track the number of days the car is in the state.
This column serves to warn people with out-of-state license plates solely for evading taxes and emissions rules (and those thinking about doing it) to reconsider. Eventually, more efficient enforcement mechanisms such as Utah’s will be coming to other states. Police may step up enforcement efforts either through direct traffic stops or indirectly by targeting street takeovers, noise regulation violations, or in car accidents due to dangerous driving.
I understand that some people think the laws are oppressive or even unconstitutional. I also understand that it may be unfair to tax some cars that are only driven a few times per year due to its collectible status or historical significance. If that is the case, organize your car enthusiast friends and contact your state representative or challenge the rules in court.
Steven Chung is a tax attorney in Los Angeles, California. He helps people with basic tax planning and resolve tax disputes. He is also sympathetic to people with large student loans. He can be reached via email at stevenchungatl@gmail.com. Or you can connect with him on Twitter (@stevenchung) and connect with him on LinkedIn.

articles.title: Federalist Society & Bari Weiss University Planning New Law School… Move Over ASSLaw!
articles.content:
Politicians started chipping away at the American Bar Association’s law school accreditation authority over the last several months. First, a number of states — including, importantly, Texas — announced that they would stop respecting the ABA’s century of experience vetting legal education. Then the federal government stepped in, with the FTC disingenuously claiming ABA accreditation contributes to rising tuition, followed by the Education Department recommending yanking the ABA’s federal recognition altogether.
Now we’re getting our first look at what an unregulated legal education environment might look like and of course it involves the Federalist Society and Bari Weiss University.
The University of Austin was founded by, among others, Weiss and Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale and marketed — sometimes explicitly and sometimes stealthily — as an “anti-woke” institution. Basically, the school offers an unaccredited safe space for students who want to read John Locke inside an echo chamber of vapid culture war tropes. Which, of course, closely resembles the hellscape that Weiss — who has said that the ideological spectrum of acceptable discourse should run from Alan Dershowitz to Dana Loesch — hopes to midwife.
Larry Summers was once on the advisory board for this school and walked away because he was “not comfortable with the course that UATX has set.” That dude couldn’t walk away from Jeffrey Epstein but took a hard pass on this university.
As functionally a series of right-wing TEDx talks dressed up as a school, the University of Austin doesn’t have a law school yet, but it has big plans to bring one online as early as 2028. And it took its first step down that road with a Substack manifesto titled: “Save the Constitution. Ditch the ABA,” announcing that it is teaming up with the Federalist Society to build a new undergrad law program as a precursor to a full law school.
UATX general counsel Adam Biggs describes it as “building the future of legal education,” which is fair in that dystopias are a kind of “future.”
We begin in the undergrad program because the people who will defend the Constitution are formed before they set foot in law school. With the Federalist Society’s support, we are deepening what we offer our undergraduates with new courses that go further into the Constitution’s text, history, and tradition, taught by judges, practicing lawyers, and scholars. We will host debates on the biggest legal questions shaping society. This will be the most substantial learning experience any student interested in law can have anywhere.
Ooooooh. You took an undergrad constitutional law course? Guys, drop everything, we’ve got to admit this kid with a con law survey course from an unaccredited school run out of an office building!
For decades, the Federalist Society has maintained that it’s just a social club for students to get together, listen to salon-style debates, and performatively eat Chick-fil-A to own the libs. In reality, the group has taken on a leading role in the “No More Souters”-industrial complex, serving as the default vetting and networking pipeline for the right-wing legal movement. It’s a branding that they’ve enforced hard enough that in 2022, they told co-founder Steven Calabresi he could no longer call himself a “founder” after he committed limited ideological heresy. Now they’re drawing up plans for a full curriculum to become a sort of bargain bin PragerU law school.
To some degree, the Federalist Society is suffering the same fate as the ABA. Last May, Trump called Federalist Society honcho Leonard Leo a “sleazebag” who “probably hates America” after Trump appointees had the temerity to rule against him. That said, no one really thinks the Federalist Society has lost its prized position in the conservative legal movement pipeline. Its establishment voices may carry less weight with this administration than they did in the past, but Federalist Society bona fides remain a necessary if no longer sufficient condition within the movement.
Keeping the Constitution demands lawyers who understand its original meaning, and fewer and fewer do. At the University of Austin (UATX), we built a tuition-free undergraduate program to form citizens and leaders who not only know our founding principles but will defend them. But the country needs a bigger, bolder version of that program, one that forms its future lawyers the same way. We will build it, and we cannot let anyone stand in the way, least of all the American Bar Association (ABA).
Yes, the problem is the shortage of judges obsessed with “original meaning.”
At least the post foregrounds its interest in setting up a program more focused on ideology than actually learning the law. It will take detours to indulge the canard that ABA accreditation drives up tuition — as opposed to U.S. News ranking criteria and cuts to support for public institutions. The ABA admitted its standards contributed to higher faculty salaries, but comparing a 5 percent faculty raise to building new high-tech student centers for the brochures is… well, sort of like comparing the University of Austin to the University of Texas at Austin.
Though it’s not clear why any of this would matter to the University of Austin since they’re tuition free, backed by a $100 million donation from Jeff Yass. Scolding the education system for high costs reads less genuine when it’s coming from a school funded on billionaire bucks.
Then there are the clinics, which act as small law firms inside the law school. The ABA’s standards make creating clinics largely unavoidable.
Students working real cases sounds good, in the abstract. Yet it is the most expensive way to teach anything. A professor teaching Property reaches hundreds of students. A clinical professor works with about eight.
Nothing says you’ve got your finger on the pulse of the issues facing legal education like a hard stance against practical training. Law firms have started hiring fewer graduates — well, fewer students… they aren’t even waiting for them to graduate anymore — and the conventional wisdom is that artificial intelligence will drive down the need for young associates even further. And with that, the burden of practical training, which historically skewed more toward the firms, may shift back onto the law schools. Meanwhile, the Federalist Society is eyeing a curriculum with more lecture halls.
Good luck with that.
But then, like salmon returning to the rivers where they were spawned, the post gets back to culture war grievances:
The entrenchment of these politics has likewise led to a deeper failure at these institutions. Too many students now graduate fluent in critical theory yet strangers to the Federalist Papers, trained to critique the Constitution before they understand the tradition that produced it. The grievance-based study of the law undermines the pursuit of truth and instills the belief that the Constitution and our republic are obstacles to be torn down.
“Fluent in critical theory yet strangers to the Federalist Papers” plays well to a cable news audience of non-lawyers, but it should face a steep challenge to anyone whose brain isn’t completely cooked. A more fair description of law school would be “fluent in comparative negligence yet strangers to the Federalist Papers” because the former has a lot more relevance to the actual lived experience of attending law school than either alternative.
But even with Texas breaking from the ABA on law school accreditation, the state supreme court couched its move in terms that could pose problems for this plan. When that court took the accreditation job itself in January, it went out of its way to promise it would seek to preserve the ability of its graduates to use their Texas degrees in other states. Which means Texas cannot approve a school built on the explicit premise of ignoring national standards without breaking from the framework it laid out over the winter.
You guys, I don’t think ASSLaw has anything to worry about.
